transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-23
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Nina Patel (AE), Marco Ruiz (SE), Sophie Chen
Attendees (Customer): Jamal Price (Head of ML), Rebecca Lin (Infra), Omar Khalid (CTO), Ana Gomez (PM)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Strandline's p95 latency targets, concurrency needs, streaming behavior and whether hosted, dedicated, or private deployment is the right fit. Customer is preparing a user-facing assistant with mixed short/long responses and sporadic bursts at product launches. Wants concrete token/sec benchmarks and fallback behavior for peak traffic.

Topics covered:
- p95 latency targets by request type (short prompts vs long streaming completions)
- Concurrency and burst sizing (typical steady-state, expected peaks, and cold starts)
- Hosting mode tradeoffs: Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Token/sec benchmarking plan and what artifacts Redwood needs
- Security controls: KMS, SOC2, audit logs, SSO/SAML, data residency
- Next steps and POC timeline

Action items (captured in metadata): see action_items field

Transcript:
[00:00] Nina Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining—uh we're looking forward to learning about Strandline's target p95s and how you want to run inference. I'm Nina, AE on this account. Marco's our systems SE and will dig into benchmarks.
[00:09] Jamal Price: Hey thanks, Nina. Quick intro, I'm Jamal, we run the ML platform at Strandline. Rebecca is infra, Omar our CTO, and Ana is the product owner. We want to see if Redwood hosted or dedicated is viable, and what it'd take to run private later.
[00:24] Marco Ruiz: Great. Can you describe your workload distribution? Short yes/no prompts, long streaming responses, lots of embeddings? Helps us size.
[00:31] Jamal Price: It's mixed. 70% short user queries (~20-60 tokens), 20% long streaming responses for assistant flows (200-1200 tokens), and 10% embeddings for search batching. In peak launches we saw surges up 6x baseline for 15-30 minutes.
[00:48] Rebecca Lin: Also we care about p95 because our UX folks measure p95 end-to-end, want it under 400ms for short queries. For streaming completions p95 is trickier, we want the first token to be under 250ms, then steady token throughput.
[01:05] Sophie Chen: Cool, first-token p95 under 250ms for streaming is a helpful constraint. Do you have a current metric for your backend inference?
[01:12] Ana Gomez: We have some numbers from our current infra—on-prem cluster with mixed GPUs. Short prompt p95 is ~600ms right now, first-stream token p95 about 480ms, and sustained token/sec is variable because our batching logic isn't great.
[01:28] Marco Ruiz: Okay. Two things to call out upfront—latency for short prompts depends on model size, quantization and batching; and streaming first-token often suffers from cold KV cache and model load time. We can do optimizations (hot-warm pools, serving warmed with KV cache, and continuous batching) but tradeoffs exist with cost.
[01:47] Jamal Price: What's the typical delta between hosted and dedicated for p95? We care about predictability more than lowest price.
[01:53] Nina Patel: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value; we have multi-tenant pools with strong isolation but not dedicated hardware. For strict p95 SLAs and guaranteed throughput dedicated is the right path—reserved GPU pools, predictable tail latency, and reserved burst capacity. We can share SLO numbers from similar customers.
[02:09] Marco Ruiz: For example, for a 7B-class model, hosted p95 for short prompts often sits around 250-350ms in our regions; on dedicated with optimized kernels and pinned NVMe/KV caches you can push p95 under 220ms reliably at modest concurrency. Larger models (70B) change the story—p95 climbs and token/sec decreases.
[02:29] Omar Khalid: We're evaluating a 13B model for assistant baseline. How do you benchmark token/sec for streaming? We need a reproducible harness.
[02:36] Marco Ruiz: We usually run two suites: 1) endpoint (batching) benchmarks with steady-state concurrency patterns, measuring p50/p95/p99, and 2) streaming token throughput with a replayed trace at realistic seqlens to capture first-token and sustained token/sec. We'll provide a harness (k6-based + python runner) and an instruction on capture format.
[02:55] Jamal Price: Sounds good, can you support tokenization differences? We tokenize differently at times.
[03:00] Marco Ruiz: Yes, send us a sample of your tokenization mapping or raw prompts. We will run with same tokenizer and same prompt shapes.
[03:06] Rebecca Lin: For PII, we need to know about data at rest and logs—do you send customer data to Redwood control plane for hosted? What about KMS?
[03:15] Nina Patel: Hosted stores minimal telemetry—request metadata for billing and observability. Customers can enable sidecar encryption; our hosted environment supports customer-managed KMS for keys. For Dedicated and Private you can use your own KMS/HSM and logs remain in your VPC. We'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[03:33] Ana Gomez: If we choose private later, how much work to migrate? We may want to start hosted, test benchmarks, and then move to dedicated or private.
[03:41] Marco Ruiz: Migration is planned: same API and runtime abstraction. You pin model versions and rollout policies. Private requires network setup (VPC peering, firewall rules) and some infra ops for the control plane. We have an onboarding checklist we can run with your infra team.
[03:58] Jamal Price: On cold starts—if we have a launch spike, can Redwood autoscale fast enough? We cannot accept long tails for the first 30 minutes.
[04:05] Marco Ruiz: We offer burst capacity options with dedicated pools—warm standby instances to handle short spikes. For hosted, we have smart routing and try fast fallbacks to smaller quantized variants to keep latency low, but there's a chance of slight tail expansion on huge surges.
[04:22] Rebecca Lin: Fallbacks to quantized model variants could affect quality; we need to know the quality delta.
[04:27] Sophie Chen: We can run subjective evals on your prompt sets during the POC. Redwood Optimize provides quantization recommendations and helps choose acceptable quality thresholds. We'll tie evals to regression alerts.
[04:40] Jamal Price: Ok what do you need from us to run the bench?
[04:43] Marco Ruiz: Sample prompt set, tokenization mapping, definition of p95 (client observed vs end-to-end), and a replay trace for burst scenarios. Also the model sizes you want tested (13B baseline + maybe 70B variant).
[04:55] Ana Gomez: We'll share traces and our p95 definitions. Regarding compliance, we need audit logs and SSO—are those available for dedicated?
[05:02] Nina Patel: Yes, dedicated and private support SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs exported to your SIEM, and retention policies. We'll include details in the security pack.
[05:14] Jamal Price: Competitor question: how is Redwood different vs just self-hosting? We have internal ops, but building all the inference orchestration is a big lift.
[05:22] Marco Ruiz: Win for Redwood: we provide a serving runtime optimized for continuous batching, KV cache management, and optimized kernels. Plus the orchestration layer—routing, canary rollouts, fallback policies—so you don't rebuild dev ops. Dedicated gives you predictable economics without designing autoscaling from scratch.
[05:39] Rebecca Lin: Pricing question—how does dedicated pricing work for reserved capacity and burst?
[05:44] Nina Patel: We offer monthly reserved capacity with configurable burst credits. We'll send a pricing matrix with example scenarios (steady-state 200 rps, peak 1200 rps, etc.) so you can model unit economics.
[05:55] Jamal Price: Great. Technical: do you support custom kernels or specific NVIDIA drivers for on-prem?
[05:59] Marco Ruiz: For private on-prem we support a curated set of drivers and kernels; you can run our package. For Dedicated we manage drivers and kernel selection. We also have a quantization-friendly path for INT8/4 where applicable.
[06:10] Ana Gomez: One friction we anticipate is observability. We need token-level cost and latency breakdowns.
[06:15] Sophie Chen: Redwood Console gives per-route token cost, model-level latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks. We can integrate with your Grafana/Datadog.
[06:23] Jamal Price: Ok, good. Any gotchas for streaming over flaky networks? We must tolerate intermittent mobile client disconnects.
[06:29] Marco Ruiz: We recommend client-side reconnect with resume tokens; on the server side we keep KV cache and allow retried transcripts. For mobile, you can prefer shorter chunks and prefetch where possible.
[06:40] Nina Patel: To recap real quick—Strandline wants first-token streaming p95 under 250ms, short prompt p95 under 400ms, and reliable burst handling up to 6x baseline. Action items: we'll send pricing, benchmark plan, and security docs. Customer will share traces and tokenization. Schedule POC next week.
[06:58] Jamal Price: Sounds right. Rebecca will collect traces. Omars okay with timeline.
[07:03] Omar Khalid: Yes, let's run the harness on a 13B and see economics. If numbers look good we may commit to a short dedicated pilot.
[07:10] Nina Patel: Perfect. We'll follow up with an email including Doodle for the kickoff and attach the benchmark plan.
[07:15] Jamal Price: Thanks everyone.
[07:17] Marco Ruiz: Thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription fidelity: occasional speaker overlaps, some technical terms transcribed imperfectly ("KV cash" for KV cache, "quantize four" instead of "quantized 4-bit"), and timestamps approximate.
